schools.summary: Henry dwells on Esther's boldness: the fast finished, she loses no time; a heart enlarged in communion is emboldened; she puts on royal robes to please her husband, abhorring the sign of her high estate, and stands between hope and fear.
Keil and Delitzsch stage the scene (royal apparel, the inner court over against the throne); Ellicott fixes the third day as the fast of Esther 4:16 and renders 'royal apparel' literally 'royalty.'
Gill reckons it the third day of the fast, notes the Targum's 'third day of the passover' (16 Nisan), and the fast of Esther fixed on 13 Adar.
Clarke takes it as the third day of the fast prescribed to Mordecai and the Jews.

themes: the third day of the fast
the bold approach to the king

schools.summary: Clarke relays the Septuagint's fuller scene (the king first enraged, Esther fainting, the sceptre laid on her neck) and Xenophon's maxim that faithful friends, not the golden sceptre, save a kingdom; Wesley reads the sceptre held out and touched as pardon offered and thankfully received.
Gill marks the peril of coming uncalled after thirty days unsummoned (Vashti divorced for less), yet the king's heart, held in God's hand, inclined to her.
Keil and Delitzsch describe the act plainly: she obtained favour, the king held out the golden sceptre, and she touched (probably kissed, with the Vulgate) its top.
Henry: the sceptre protected her from the law; having power with God like Jacob, she had power with men, for he that will lose his life for God shall save it.

themes: the king's heart in God's hand
power with God and with men

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the king inferring some urgent matter and promising 'to the half of the kingdom'; Ellicott traces the extravagant offer through Esther 5:6 and 7:2 and its echo in Herod's promise (Mark 6:23).

Henry turns the exchange into an encouragement to prayer (Luke 18:6-8): if a proud king so promises, will not God hear his elect? — believers come invited, with a promise and an Advocate, so come boldly to the throne of grace.
Wesley reads 'to the half of the kingdom' as proverbial (nothing in reason denied), and 'it shall be given' as God preventing fears and outdoing hopes.
Gill: the king supposed she had some business or suit to lay before him.

themes: to the half of the kingdom
boldness at the throne of grace

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note she invited Haman deliberately, to accuse him to his face (Calovius); Ellicott reads her temporising to gain time and a favourable moment, and marks the shift from 'let the king come' to the direct 'in thy sight, O king.'
Clarke judges Haman invited to prevent his suspicion and any hasty step; Wesley reads the courtesy to the favourite as a way to insinuate herself into the king's affection.

Henry gathers her aims into one prudence — to value his company, try his affection, soften his spirit, please him through Haman, and gain a fairer opportunity; wisdom takes hard men by the right handle.
Gill: she humbly submits the matter to the king's pleasure.
Gill: the king bade his servants make haste to acquaint Haman with the invitation and press him to comply.
Keil and Delitzsch gloss 'cause Haman to make haste' as the king sending to fetch him quickly, that the queen's word be carried out.
Henry reads the king's ready coming, and his ordering Haman along, as a token of the kindness he still bore Esther — he would not have accepted her banquet had he meant her people's ruin.
Clarke sets it at the point when wine was introduced; Wesley explains the 'banquet of wine' as fruits and wines rather than meats, an entertainment frequent among the Persians.

Ellicott calls it the continuation of the banquet of v.5, the dessert; Keil and Delitzsch mark the king repeating his question in the greatest cheerfulness, renewing the pledge of v.3 with an optative 'it shall be done.'
Gill describes the two Persian courses (meats with water, then fruits with wine, from Aelian), the king accosting the queen over the second.
Henry hears the same open generosity of the throne, the proverbial 'half the kingdom' by which the king would deny nothing in reason (cf. Herod, Mark 6:23).

Keil and Delitzsch trace the broken sentence — 'My petition and my request —' then the deferral to a second banquet; Haman was invited both times (Calovius) that Esther might arraign him in the king's presence and shut off every escape.

Henry ascribes the delay first to prudence (to win further upon the king, perhaps her heart failing, desiring more time for prayer), noting what is asked with a pause deserves to be considered — then above all to God putting it into her heart.
Gill: she names her petition but for wise reasons still defers the principal request, offering only a lesser thing for the present.

Clarke: she was gaining on the king's affections but not yet confident, so wished another interview; Wesley allows the prudence but adds she may have been daunted, her courage failing — both subordinating the delay to a Providence keeping room for the coming night.
Henry: God put it into Esther's heart to delay a day longer; she knew not, but God knew, what was to happen that very night.
Gill reads 'if I have found favour' as a settled certainty, proved by the sceptre and the accepted banquet.
Keil and Delitzsch give the plain sense of the postponement — come to-morrow, and 'I will do as the king hath said,' i.e. make known the request.

debates.question: Why did Esther defer her petition to a second banquet?

sides.position: deliberate prudence — to gain confidence, ingratiate herself, and show reverence, what is asked with a pause being the better weighed
a failure of nerve — she was daunted in the king's presence and her courage of utterance failed her

themes: to-morrow I will do as the king said

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark Haman joyful until Mordecai neither stood up nor trembled; Ellicott judges that Mordecai's earlier honourable refusal to bow (Esther 3:2) here hardens into indefensible rudeness.

Wesley reads Mordecai's stillness as faith — showing how little he feared Haman and how firm his confidence in God; Clarke grants an inflexibility carried to its highest pitch, supposing some reverence was owed that he could not conscientiously pay.
Henry reads it as conscience — he that walks uprightly walks surely — and lingers on the affront as the dead fly spoiling Haman's ointment, the bottomless discontent of pride.
Gill notes Haman went from court joyful and glad of heart.

debates.question: How is Mordecai's refusal to rise or move for Haman to be judged?

sides.position: faithful steadfastness — an act of conscience and of confidence in God
indefensible rudeness — his earlier honourable independence here degenerates
inflexibility at its highest pitch, though some reverence was arguably required

themes: the dead fly in the ointment

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: Haman refrained himself and went home to summon friends and Zeresh for counsel; Ellicott glosses Zeresh (a Persian word for 'gold,' the Targum's daughter of Tatnai, Ezra 5:3).
Wesley sees God's providence disposing Haman's heart against its own inclination, making him fasten fetters on his own hands rather than take easy vengeance.
Gill: Haman thought it beneath him to avenge himself on one man when the whole people would soon feel his hand.
Henry hears the inward war — anger demanding blood, malice waiting for the appointed day — thorns and snares in the way of the froward.

Keil and Delitzsch confirm the wealth and the ten sons (Esther 9:7-10), many sons esteemed among the Persians (Herodotus), and the promotion above the princes (Esther 3:1); Ellicott hears mere vain-glory — the pride that goeth before destruction.
Gill: Haman told of his riches in ostentation and to ease his mortification, aggravating that a man of such wealth was slighted by one Jew; ten sons, esteemed among the Persians.
Clarke notes the Asiatic delight in a multitude of children, a reason for their many wives and concubines.
Henry: Haman thought the queen meant to honour him, whereas she meant to accuse him — calling him to the banquet was calling him to the bar; self-flatterers are self-deceivers (Obad. 3).
Wesley: he makes a matter of glorying of the very thing that would prove his ruin — the wisest of men rejoicing in what they most have cause to fear.
Keil and Delitzsch give the boast: none but Haman admitted to the banquet with the king, and invited again on the morrow.
Gill: to all the rest Haman added what delighted him most, a fresh and singular honour.

themes: the sole guest of king and queen
called to the bar, not to honour

schools.summary: Wesley: though proud men have much to their mind, if not all it is nothing — the thousandth part would content a humble man; Clarke preaches that the soul was made for God and nothing but God can fill it, citing Solomon, Ahab, and Haman wretched amid his honours.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'not equalled to me,' not answering his desires; Ellicott sharpens 'availeth me nothing' to 'suiteth me not, contenteth me not.'
Gill: no abundance is sufficient — it gives him no satisfaction, no contentment.

Keil and Delitzsch lay out the counsel — a tree fifty cubits high, Mordecai impaled upon it (cf. Esther 2:23), the king sure to consent, the stake high to be seen the farther; Ellicott presses that the word means tree or structure, crucifixion doubtless meant, the Greek word the NT's for the Saviour's cross, the Latin 'crucem.'

Clarke: the word is simply wood, a tree or pole, ~75 feet, impaling rather than hanging, for greater ignominy and public spectacle; Wesley: the great height to make it conspicuous and strike Haman's enemies with dread.
Gill supposes Zeresh first moved the counsel, all his friends approving and uniting in it.
